complainant: Jo (resident with the greatest heat exposure)
source_quotes: "Plan C cools Jo's home, which has the greatest heat exposure of any home in this case"
"Jo's home is not cooled by A or B."
complaint: Plan B leaves me – the resident whose home has the single greatest heat exposure – entirely without relief during a dangerous heat-wave, whereas Plan C would remove that life-threatening risk at the cost of closing Sal’s shop for eight weeks and withholding cooling from twelve other households.  Extreme residential heat can imperil basic bodily functioning just as surely as loss of shelter or livelihood; a principle that permits the council to ignore the *worst* unmitigated heat risk when a feasible alternative could eliminate it is reasonably rejectable from my position.  The fact that twelve households would forgo a *moderate* benefit under Plan C does not explain why my unmitigated, severe heat burden may be left wholly in place; nor is it clear that Sal’s temporary income loss is weightier than imminent health-and-safety threats to me.  Therefore, the inference that Plan B is “not reasonably rejectable” fails to take my basic-needs risk seriously enough.
target_quote: Plan B is not reasonably rejectable given the available alternatives.
challenged_inference: That the continuing, unmitigated extreme-heat burden on Jo is not a severe basic-needs loss sufficient to render the principle permitting Plan B reasonably rejectable, given that an alternative (Plan C) could lift that burden.
why_prior_answer_is_insufficient: The prior answer simply labels the heat burden on Jo (and on the eight uncool households) as “weaker” than Mira’s homelessness without examining whether *Jo’s* burden is comparably severe to Sal’s income loss or to the benefits foregone by the twelve households.  It gives no contractualist reason why a life-threatening environmental hazard should count as only a moderate inconvenience, nor why a principle that sacrifices the most exposed resident’s basic safety is justifiable when another feasible plan could eliminate that risk.  Hence Jo’s complaint remains unresolved yet directly targets the claim that Plan B is not reasonably rejectable.
selection_limits: One principled, grounded complaint from Jo against the recommendation of Plan B relative to the live alternative Plan C has been articulated without inventing further facts or asserting veto power.
